claim: AtAtm3 has been implicated in the maturation of cytosolic iron-sulfur proteins.
source: The ATP binding cassette (ABC) transporter of mitochondria (Atm) from Arabidopsis thaliana (AtAtm3) has been implicated in the maturation of cytosolic iron-sulfur proteins and heavy metal detoxification, plausibly by exporting glutathione derivatives.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known function of AtAtm3.

claim: AtAtm3 has been implicated in heavy metal detoxification.
source: The ATP binding cassette (ABC) transporter of mitochondria (Atm) from Arabidopsis thaliana (AtAtm3) has been implicated in the maturation of cytosolic iron-sulfur proteins and heavy metal detoxification, plausibly by exporting glutathione derivatives.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known function of AtAtm3.

claim: AtAtm3 plausibly exports glutathione derivatives.
source: The ATP binding cassette (ABC) transporter of mitochondria (Atm) from Arabidopsis thaliana (AtAtm3) has been implicated in the maturation of cytosolic iron-sulfur proteins and heavy metal detoxification, plausibly by exporting glutathione derivatives.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the mechanism of AtAtm3 function.

claim: Four structures of AtAtm3 in three different conformational states were determined using single-particle cryo-electron microscopy.
source: Using single-particle cryo-electron microscopy, we have determined four structures of AtAtm3 in three different conformational states: two inward-facing conformations (with and without bound oxidized glutathione [GSSG]), together with closed and outward-facing states stabilized by MgADP-VO4.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by structural data throughout the manuscript.

claim: AtAtm3 structures include two inward-facing conformations with and without bound GSSG.
source: Using single-particle cryo-electron microscopy, we have determined four structures of AtAtm3 in three different conformational states: two inward-facing conformations (with and without bound oxidized glutathione [GSSG]), together with closed and outward-facing states stabilized by MgADP-VO4.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by structural data in Figure 2.

claim: AtAtm3 structures include closed and outward-facing states stabilized by MgADP-VO4.
source: Using single-particle cryo-electron microscopy, we have determined four structures of AtAtm3 in three different conformational states: two inward-facing conformations (with and without bound oxidized glutathione [GSSG]), together with closed and outward-facing states stabilized by MgADP-VO4.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by structural data in Figure 2.

claim: The AtAtm3 structures provide a structural framework for defining the alternating access transport cycle.
source: These structures not only provide a structural framework for defining the alternating access transport cycle, but also reveal the paucity of cysteine residues in the glutathione binding site that could potentially form inhibitory mixed disulfides with GSSG.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The glutathione binding site in AtAtm3 has a paucity of cysteine residues that could potentially form inhibitory mixed disulfides with GSSG.
source: These structures not only provide a structural framework for defining the alternating access transport cycle, but also reveal the paucity of cysteine residues in the glutathione binding site that could potentially form inhibitory mixed disulfides with GSSG.
evidence: This is a finding from structural analysis and sequence alignment presented in Figure 5.

claim: The ternary complex of AtAtm3 containing both GSSG and MgATP could not be prepared despite extensive efforts.
source: Despite extensive efforts, we were unable to prepare the ternary complex of AtAtm3 containing both GSSG and MgATP.
evidence: This is a negative result reported from experimental attempts.

claim: Nucleotides are found associated with all conformational states of type IV ABC transporters.
source: A survey of structurally characterized type IV ABC transporters that includes AtAtm3 establishes that while nucleotides are found associated with all conformational states, they are effectively required to stabilize occluded, closed, and outward-facing conformations.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the PCA analysis of 80 half-transporters presented in Figure 6.

claim: Nucleotides are effectively required to stabilize occluded, closed, and outward-facing conformations of type IV ABC transporters.
source: A survey of structurally characterized type IV ABC transporters that includes AtAtm3 establishes that while nucleotides are found associated with all conformational states, they are effectively required to stabilize occluded, closed, and outward-facing conformations.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the PCA analysis presented in Figure 6.

claim: Transport substrates have only been observed associated with inward-facing conformations of type IV ABC transporters.
source: In contrast, transport substrates have only been observed associated with inward-facing conformations.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the PCA analysis presented in Figure 6c.

claim: The absence of structures with dimerized nucleotide binding domains containing both nucleotide and transport substrate suggests that this form of the ternary complex exists only transiently during the transport cycle.
source: The absence of structures with dimerized nucleotide binding domains containing both nucleotide and transport substrate suggests that this form of the ternary complex exists only transiently during the transport cycle.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of such structures in the survey of type IV ABC transporters.

claim: ScAtm1 is present in the inner membrane of mitochondria.
source: The best characterized member is Saccharomyces cerevisiae Atm1 (ScAtm1) present in the inner membrane of mitochondria (Leighton and Schatz, 1995) and required for the formation of cytosolic iron-sulfur cluster containing proteins (Kispal et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Leighton and Schatz, 1995.

claim: ScAtm1 is required for the formation of cytosolic iron-sulfur cluster containing proteins.
source: The best characterized member is Saccharomyces cerevisiae Atm1 (ScAtm1) present in the inner membrane of mitochondria (Leighton and Schatz, 1995) and required for the formation of cytosolic iron-sulfur cluster containing proteins (Kispal et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kispal et al., 1999.

claim: Defects in ScAtm1 lead to an overaccumulation of iron in the mitochondria.
source: Defects in ScAtm1 lead to an overaccumulation of iron in the mitochondria (Kispal et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kispal et al., 1997.

claim: Atm1 is proposed to transport a sulfur containing intermediate.
source: Atm1 is proposed to transport a sulfur containing intermediate (Kispal et al., 1999) that may also include iron (Pandey et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kispal et al., 1999 and Pandey et al., 2019.

claim: Atm1 is likely to transport a similar sulfur containing species from the mitochondria that is required for the cytoplasmic thiolation of tRNA.
source: It is also likely to transport a similar sulfur containing species from the mitochondria that is required for the cytoplasmic thiolation of tRNA (Pandey et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pandey et al., 2018.

claim: Derivatives of glutathione have been implicated as substrates for Atm1 based on their ability to stimulate the ATPase activity of Atm1.
source: While the precise substrate that is transported remains unknown, derivatives of glutathione have been implicated based on their ability to stimulate the ATPase activity of Atm1 (Kuhnke et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kuhnke et al., 2006.

claim: Structures for Atm family members are currently available for ScAtm1, NaAtm1, and human ABCB6.
source: Structures for Atm family members are currently available for ScAtm1 (Srinivasan et al., 2014), the bacterial homolog NaAtm1 from Novosphingobium aromaticivorans (Lee et al., 2014) and human ABCB6 (Wang et al., 2020); the pairwise sequence identities between these homologous transporters range from 40% to 46%.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Srinivasan et al., 2014, Lee et al., 2014, and Wang et al., 2020.

claim: The pairwise sequence identities between ScAtm1, NaAtm1, and human ABCB6 range from 40% to 46%.
source: Structures for Atm family members are currently available for ScAtm1 (Srinivasan et al., 2014), the bacterial homolog NaAtm1 from Novosphingobium aromaticivorans (Lee et al., 2014) and human ABCB6 (Wang et al., 2020); the pairwise sequence identities between these homologous transporters range from 40% to 46%.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of sequence identities.

claim: Atm family members occur as homodimers of half-transporters.
source: These proteins occur as homodimers of half-transporters, where each half-transporter contains a transmembrane domain (TMD) followed by the canonical nucleotide binding domain (NBD) that defines the ABC transporter family.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the structure of Atm family members.

claim: Each half-transporter contains a transmembrane domain (TMD) followed by the canonical nucleotide binding domain (NBD).
source: These proteins occur as homodimers of half-transporters, where each half-transporter contains a transmembrane domain (TMD) followed by the canonical nucleotide binding domain (NBD) that defines the ABC transporter family.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the structure of ABC transporters.

claim: Each TMD consists of six transmembrane helices (TMs) that exhibit the exporter type I fold first observed for Sav1866.
source: Each TMD consists of six transmembrane helices (TMs) that exhibit the exporter type I fold first observed for Sav1866 (Dawson and Locher, 2006); a recent re-classification now identifies this group as type IV ABC transporters (Thomas et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dawson and Locher, 2006 and Thomas et al., 2020.

claim: The exporter type I fold is now classified as type IV ABC transporters.
source: Each TMD consists of six transmembrane helices (TMs) that exhibit the exporter type I fold first observed for Sav1866 (Dawson and Locher, 2006); a recent re-classification now identifies this group as type IV ABC transporters (Thomas et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Thomas et al., 2020.

claim: The translocation of substrates across the membrane proceeds through an alternating access mechanism involving the ATP-dependent interconversion between inward- and outward-facing conformational states.
source: The translocation of substrates across the membrane proceeds through an alternating access mechanism involving the ATP-dependent interconversion between inward- and outward-facing conformational states.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ABC transporter mechanisms.

claim: Among the Atm1 family, conformations have been most extensively characterized for NaAtm1 and include the occluded and closed states.
source: Among the Atm1 family, these conformations have been most extensively characterized for NaAtm1 and include the occluded and closed states that provide a structural framework for the unidirectional transport cycle (Fan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fan et al., 2020.

claim: Structures of ScAtm1 with GSH and of NaAtm1 complexed with GSH, GSSG, and GS-Hg-SG have defined the general substrate binding site in the TMD.
source: Structures of ScAtm1 with reduced glutathione (GSH) (Srinivasan et al., 2014), and of NaAtm1 complexed with reduced (GSH), oxidized (GSSG), and metallated (GS-Hg-SG) (Lee et al., 2014), have defined the general substrate binding site in the TMD for the transport substrates.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Srinivasan et al., 2014 and Lee et al., 2014.

claim: Arabidopsis has three Atm orthologues: AtAtm1, AtAtm2, and AtAtm3.
source: Plants have been found to have large numbers of transporters (Hwang et al., 2016), including Arabidopsis with three Atm orthologues, AtAtm1, AtAtm2, and AtAtm3 (Chen et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hwang et al., 2016 and Chen et al., 2007.

claim: AtAtm3 rescues the ScAtm1 phenotype.
source: Of these, AtAtm3 (also known as ABCB25) rescues the ScAtm1 phenotype (Chen et al., 2007), and has been shown to be associated with maturation of cytosolic iron-sulfur proteins (Kushnir et al., 2001), confer resistance to heavy metals such as cadmium and lead (Kim et al., 2006), and participate in the formation of molybdenum-cofactor containing enzymes (Bernard et al., 2009; Teschner et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2007.

claim: AtAtm3 has been shown to be associated with maturation of cytosolic iron-sulfur proteins.
source: Of these, AtAtm3 (also known as ABCB25) rescues the ScAtm1 phenotype (Chen et al., 2007), and has been shown to be associated with maturation of cytosolic iron-sulfur proteins (Kushnir et al., 2001), confer resistance to heavy metals such as cadmium and lead (Kim et al., 2006), and participate in the formation of molybdenum-cofactor containing enzymes (Bernard et al., 2009; Teschner et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kushnir et al., 2001.

claim: AtAtm3 confers resistance to heavy metals such as cadmium and lead.
source: Of these, AtAtm3 (also known as ABCB25) rescues the ScAtm1 phenotype (Chen et al., 2007), and has been shown to be associated with maturation of cytosolic iron-sulfur proteins (Kushnir et al., 2001), confer resistance to heavy metals such as cadmium and lead (Kim et al., 2006), and participate in the formation of molybdenum-cofactor containing enzymes (Bernard et al., 2009; Teschner et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kim et al., 2006.

claim: AtAtm3 participates in the formation of molybdenum-cofactor containing enzymes.
source: Of these, AtAtm3 (also known as ABCB25) rescues the ScAtm1 phenotype (Chen et al., 2007), and has been shown to be associated with maturation of cytosolic iron-sulfur proteins (Kushnir et al., 2001), confer resistance to heavy metals such as cadmium and lead (Kim et al., 2006), and participate in the formation of molybdenum-cofactor containing enzymes (Bernard et al., 2009; Teschner et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bernard et al., 2009 and Teschner et al., 2010.

claim: Unlike yeast, defects in AtAtm3 are not associated with iron accumulation in mitochondria.
source: Unlike yeast, defects in AtAtm3 are not associated with iron accumulation in mitochondria (Bernard et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bernard et al., 2009.

claim: AtAtm3 has been shown to transport GSSG and glutathione polysulfide.
source: While the physiological substrate is unknown, AtAtm3 has been shown to transport GSSG and glutathione polysulfide, with the persulfidated species perhaps relevant to cytosolic iron-sulfur cluster assembly (Schaedler et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schaedler et al., 2014.

claim: The ability of AtAtm3 to export GSSG has been implicated in helping stabilize against excessive glutathione oxidation in the mitochondria.
source: The ability of AtAtm3 to export GSSG has been implicated in helping stabilize against excessive glutathione oxidation in the mitochondria and thereby serving to maintain a suitable reduction potential (Marty et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Marty et al., 2019.

claim: AtAtm3 contains an N-terminal mitochondrial targeting sequence that directs the translated protein to the mitochondria.
source: AtAtm3 contains an N-terminal mitochondrial targeting sequence that directs the translated protein to the mitochondria, where it is cleaved following delivery to the inner membrane.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mitochondrial targeting sequences.

claim: The N-terminal mitochondrial targeting sequence of AtAtm3 is cleaved following delivery to the inner membrane.
source: AtAtm3 contains an N-terminal mitochondrial targeting sequence that directs the translated protein to the mitochondria, where it is cleaved following delivery to the inner membrane.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mitochondrial targeting sequences.

claim: The N-terminal targeting sequence of AtAtm3 consists of ~80 residues and is anticipated to be poorly ordered.
source: Since this targeting sequence consists of ~80 residues and is anticipated to be poorly ordered, we generated three different N-terminal truncation mutants of AtAtm3 through deletion of 60, 70, or 80 residues to identify the best-behaved construct.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of mitochondrial targeting sequences.

claim: Three different N-terminal truncation mutants of AtAtm3 were generated through deletion of 60, 70, or 80 residues.
source: Since this targeting sequence consists of ~80 residues and is anticipated to be poorly ordered, we generated three different N-terminal truncation mutants of AtAtm3 through deletion of 60, 70, or 80 residues to identify the best-behaved construct.
evidence: This is an experimental procedure described in the manuscript.

claim: The construct with the 80 amino acids deletion showed the highest expression level and proportionally less aggregation by size exclusion chromatography.
source: The construct with the 80 amino acids deletion showed the highest expression level and proportionally less aggregation by size exclusion chromatography (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and hence was used for further functional and structural studies.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The basal ATPase activity of AtAtm3 was significantly higher in detergent than in nanodiscs (104 vs. 7.7 nmol/min/mg).
source: The basal ATPase activity, measured in the absence of glutathione derivatives, was significantly higher in detergent than in nanodiscs (104 vs. 7.7 nmol/min/mg, respectively; Figure 1ab), while the apparent Kms for MgATP were within a factor of two (~0.16 and 0.08 mM, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The apparent Kms for MgATP of AtAtm3 were within a factor of two in detergent and nanodiscs (~0.16 and 0.08 mM, respectively).
source: The basal ATPase activity, measured in the absence of glutathione derivatives, was significantly higher in detergent than in nanodiscs (104 vs. 7.7 nmol/min/mg, respectively; Figure 1ab), while the apparent Kms for MgATP were within a factor of two (~0.16 and 0.08 mM, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: In nanodiscs, the ATPase rates of AtAtm3 increase to 32 and 39 nmol/min/mg with 2.5 mM GSSG and 10 mM GSH, respectively.
source: In nanodiscs, the ATPase rates increase to 32 and 39 nmol/min/mg with 2.5 mM GSSG and 10 mM GSH, respectively, for an overall increase of 4–5× above the basal rate.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: In nanodiscs, GSSG and GSH stimulate the ATPase activity of AtAtm3 by 4-5× above the basal rate.
source: In nanodiscs, the ATPase rates increase to 32 and 39 nmol/min/mg with 2.5 mM GSSG and 10 mM GSH, respectively, for an overall increase of 4–5× above the basal rate.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The ATPase rates for AtAtm3 in DDM increase to 117 and 154 nmol/min/mg with GSSG and GSH, respectively.
source: The ATPase rates for AtAtm3 in DDM also increase with GSSG and GSH, to 117 and 154 nmol/min/mg, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The structure of AtAtm3 reconstituted in nanodiscs in the absence of nucleotide or transport substrate was determined at 3.4 Å resolution.
source: We first determined the structure of AtAtm3 reconstituted in nanodiscs at 3.4 Å resolution in the absence of either nucleotide or transport substrate (Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary structural finding supported by Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The apo structure of AtAtm3 revealed an inward-facing conformation similar to those observed for ScAtm1 and NaAtm1.
source: This structure revealed an inward-facing conformation for AtAtm3 similar to those observed for the inward-facing conformations for ScAtm1 (PDB ID: 4myc) and NaAtm1 (PDB ID: 6vqu) with overall alignment root mean square deviations (rmsds) for the dimer of 2.6 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a, b) and 2.1 Å (Figure 2), respectively, and half-transporter alignment rmsds of 2.3 and 2.0 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 2c), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparisons shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The overall alignment rmsd between the apo AtAtm3 structure and ScAtm1 (PDB ID: 4myc) is 2.6 Å for the dimer.
source: This structure revealed an inward-facing conformation for AtAtm3 similar to those observed for the inward-facing conformations for ScAtm1 (PDB ID: 4myc) and NaAtm1 (PDB ID: 6vqu) with overall alignment root mean square deviations (rmsds) for the dimer of 2.6 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a, b) and 2.1 Å (Figure 2), respectively, and half-transporter alignment rmsds of 2.3 and 2.0 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 2c), respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative structural comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The overall alignment rmsd between the apo AtAtm3 structure and NaAtm1 (PDB ID: 6vqu) is 2.1 Å for the dimer.
source: This structure revealed an inward-facing conformation for AtAtm3 similar to those observed for the inward-facing conformations for ScAtm1 (PDB ID: 4myc) and NaAtm1 (PDB ID: 6vqu) with overall alignment root mean square deviations (rmsds) for the dimer of 2.6 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a, b) and 2.1 Å (Figure 2), respectively, and half-transporter alignment rmsds of 2.3 and 2.0 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 2c), respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative structural comparison shown in Figure 2.

claim: AtAtm3 has an approximately 20 amino acid loop between TM1 and TM2 that would be positioned in the intermembrane space.
source: The primary distinction between these structures is the presence of an approximately 20 amino acid loop between TM1 and TM2 of AtAtm3 that would be positioned in the intermembrane space and is absent from the structures of ABCB7 (Jumper et al., 2021; Varadi et al., 2022), ABCB6 (Song et al., 2021), ScAtm1 (Srinivasan et al., 2014), and NaAtm1 (Lee et al., 2014; Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The loop between TM1 and TM2 is absent from the structures of ABCB7, ABCB6, ScAtm1, and NaAtm1.
source: The primary distinction between these structures is the presence of an approximately 20 amino acid loop between TM1 and TM2 of AtAtm3 that would be positioned in the intermembrane space and is absent from the structures of ABCB7 (Jumper et al., 2021; Varadi et al., 2022), ABCB6 (Song et al., 2021), ScAtm1 (Srinivasan et al., 2014), and NaAtm1 (Lee et al., 2014; Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparisons shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and citations.

claim: A 3.6 Å resolution single-particle cryoEM structure of AtAtm3 purified in DDM with bound GSSG was determined.
source: To further look at substrate binding, we determined a 3.6 Å resolution single-particle cryoEM structure of AtAtm3 purified in DDM with bound GSSG (Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a primary structural finding supported by Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: In the GSSG-bound structure, AtAtm3 adopts an inward-facing conformation.
source: In this structure, AtAtm3 adopts an inward-facing conformation, with an overall alignment rmsd to the ligand-free inward-facing structure of 2.9 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 5a) and a corresponding half-transporter alignment rmsd of 1.6 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 5b).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: The main difference between the apo and GSSG-bound inward-facing structures is the extent of NBD dimer separation.
source: The main difference between the two structures is the extent of NBD dimer separation (Figure 2—figure supplement 5a), where the GSSG-bound structure presents a more closed NBD dimer relative to the substrate-free structure.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5a.

claim: The TM6s in the inward-facing structures of AtAtm3 adopt a kinked conformation including residues 429–438.
source: As previously noted with NaAtm1 (Fan et al., 2020), the TM6s in these inward-facing structures of AtAtm3 adopt a kinked conformation including residues 429–438 (Figure 2cd).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2c,d and citation to Fan et al., 2020.

claim: The TM6 kink opens the backbone hydrogen bonding interactions to create the binding site for GSSG.
source: This opens the backbone hydrogen bonding interactions to create the binding site for GSSG (Figure 2e) with binding pocket residues identified by PDBePISA (Krissinel and Henrick, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2e and citation to Krissinel and Henrick, 2007.

claim: The binding mode of GSSG in the AtAtm3 inward-facing conformation is similar to that observed in the inward-facing structure of the GSSG-bound NaAtm1.
source: The binding mode of GSSG in this AtAtm3 inward-facing conformation is similar to that observed in the inward-facing structure of the GSSG-bound NaAtm1 (Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a structural comparison supported by citation to Lee et al., 2014.

claim: A structure of AtAtm3 in the closed conformation with AtAtm3 reconstituted in nanodiscs at 3.9 Å resolution was determined.
source: We determined two structures of AtAtm3 stabilized with MgADP-VO4, one in the closed conformation with AtAtm3 reconstituted in nanodiscs at 3.9 Å resolution (Figure 2f and Figure 2—figure supplement 6) and the other in the outward-facing conformation with AtAtm3 in DDM at 3.8 Å resolution (Figure 2g and Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is a primary structural finding supported by Figure 2f and Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: A structure of AtAtm3 in the outward-facing conformation with AtAtm3 in DDM at 3.8 Å resolution was determined.
source: We determined two structures of AtAtm3 stabilized with MgADP-VO4, one in the closed conformation with AtAtm3 reconstituted in nanodiscs at 3.9 Å resolution (Figure 2f and Figure 2—figure supplement 6) and the other in the outward-facing conformation with AtAtm3 in DDM at 3.8 Å resolution (Figure 2g and Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is a primary structural finding supported by Figure 2g and Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claim: The closed and outward-facing structures of AtAtm3 share an overall alignment rmsd of 1.7 Å.
source: These two structures share an overall alignment rmsd of 1.7 Å with the primary difference being a change in separation of the TMs surrounding the translocation pathway on the side of the transporter facing the intermembrane space (Figure 2—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is a quantitative structural comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 8.

claim: Access to the intermembrane space is blocked in the closed conformation.
source: As a result of these changes in the TMDs, access to the intermembrane space is either blocked in the closed conformation (Figure 2f) or is open in the outward-facing conformation (Figure 2g).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: Access to the intermembrane space is open in the outward-facing conformation.
source: As a result of these changes in the TMDs, access to the intermembrane space is either blocked in the closed conformation (Figure 2f) or is open in the outward-facing conformation (Figure 2g).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2g.

claim: TM6 in the closed structure presents a kinked conformation.
source: The changes in the TMDs are reflected in the conformations of TM6, which in the closed structure presents a kinked conformation (Figure 2h), in contrast to the straight conformation in the outward-facing structure that has the backbone hydrogen bonding interaction restored in the helices (Figure 2i).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2h.

claim: TM6 in the outward-facing structure has a straight conformation with the backbone hydrogen bonding interaction restored in the helices.
source: The changes in the TMDs are reflected in the conformations of TM6, which in the closed structure presents a kinked conformation (Figure 2h), in contrast to the straight conformation in the outward-facing structure that has the backbone hydrogen bonding interaction restored in the helices (Figure 2i).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2i.

claim: The dimerized NBDs are virtually identical in the closed and outward-facing structures with an overall alignment rmsd of 0.8 Å.
source: In contrast to the variation in the TMDs, the dimerized NBDs are virtually identical in these two structures with an overall alignment rmsd of 0.8 Å (Figure 2fg and Figure 2—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is a quantitative structural comparison shown in Figure 2f,g and Figure 2—figure supplement 8.

claim: The ATPase rate measured in detergent is about fivefold greater than that measured in nanodiscs.
source: Overall, the ATPase rate measured in detergent is about fivefold greater than that measured in nanodiscs, perhaps indicative of a more tightly coupled ATPase activity in a membrane-like environment.
evidence: This is a comparison of ATPase activity data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Both GSH and GSSG stimulate the ATPase activity of AtAtm3 by increasing Vmax, with little change observed in the Km for MgATP.
source: Both GSH and GSSG stimulate the ATPase activity by increasing Vmax, with little change observed in the Km for MgATP.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the ATPase activity data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The ability of GSSG to stimulate the ATPase activity of AtAtm3 agrees with previous reports.
source: The ability of GSSG to stimulate the ATPase activity of AtAtm3 agrees with previous reports (Schaedler et al., 2014), while the stimulation we observe with 10 mM GSH differs from the lack of stimulation noted in that work with 1.7 and 3.3 mM GSH.
evidence: This is a comparison with previous work supported by citation to Schaedler et al., 2014.

claim: The stimulation of ATPase activity by 10 mM GSH differs from the lack of stimulation noted in previous work with 1.7 and 3.3 mM GSH.
source: The ability of GSSG to stimulate the ATPase activity of AtAtm3 agrees with previous reports (Schaedler et al., 2014), while the stimulation we observe with 10 mM GSH differs from the lack of stimulation noted in that work with 1.7 and 3.3 mM GSH.
evidence: This is a comparison with previous work supported by citation to Schaedler et al., 2014.

claim: The parallels between the structurally characterized conformations of AtAtm3 and NaAtm1 support the idea that these conformational states are relevant to the transport cycle.
source: The parallels between the structurally characterized conformations of AtAtm3 and NaAtm1 support the idea that these conformational states are relevant to the transport cycle, and not simply an artifact of the specific conditions used to prepare each sample.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparisons between AtAtm3 and NaAtm1.

claim: The outward-facing conformation observed for AtAtm3 had not been previously observed with NaAtm1.
source: The conformations observed for AtAtm3 and NaAtm1 do not completely correspond, however; most notably, the outward-facing conformation observed for AtAtm3 had not been previously observed with NaAtm1 (Fan et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2014), while the occluded conformations found with NaAtm1 were not observed for AtAtm3.
evidence: This is a comparison with previous work supported by citations to Fan et al., 2020 and Lee et al., 2014.

claim: The occluded conformations found with NaAtm1 were not observed for AtAtm3.
source: The conformations observed for AtAtm3 and NaAtm1 do not completely correspond, however; most notably, the outward-facing conformation observed for AtAtm3 had not been previously observed with NaAtm1 (Fan et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2014), while the occluded conformations found with NaAtm1 were not observed for AtAtm3.
evidence: This is a comparison with previous work supported by citations to Fan et al., 2020 and Lee et al., 2014.

claim: The closed conformation stabilized by MgADP-VO4 has been observed for both NaAtm1 and AtAtm3.
source: The closed conformation stabilized by MgADP-VO4 has been observed for both NaAtm1 (Fan et al., 2020) and AtAtm3.
evidence: This is a comparison supported by citation to Fan et al., 2020 and structural data for AtAtm3.

claim: In the closed conformation, the TM6s adopt a kinked conformation at residues 438–441 that eliminates the substrate binding cavity.
source: In comparing the closed and the outward-facing conformations of AtAtm3, the arrangements of the NBDs are superimposable, with the major differences between the two conformational states involving the local conformation of TM6s. In the closed conformation, the TM6s adopt a kinked conformation at residues 438–441 that eliminates the substrate binding cavity, whereas the TM6s in the outward-facing conformation present straight TM6s (Figure 2hi).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2h,i.

claim: The TM6 helical kink in the closed conformation is adjacent to, but distinct from, the helical kink present at residues 429–438 in the inward-facing conformation.
source: The TM6 helical kink in the closed conformation is adjacent to, but distinct from, the helical kink present at residues 429–438 in the inward-facing conformation.
evidence: This is a structural comparison of TM6 conformations in different states.

claim: The presence of the closed conformation in a post-ATP hydrolysis state enforces unidirectionality of the transport process by precluding the uptake of substrate from the outside.
source: By eliminating the substrate binding cavity, the presence of the closed conformation in a post-ATP hydrolysis state enforces unidirectionality of the transport process by precluding the uptake of substrate from the outside.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional role of the closed conformation.

claim: MgADP-VO4 stabilized two different conformational states for AtAtm3, the closed state in nanodiscs and the outward-facing conformation in detergent.
source: We note that MgADP-VO4 was observed to stabilize two different conformational states for AtAtm3, the closed state in nanodiscs and the outward-facing conformation in detergent (Figure 2fg).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2f,g.

claim: The stabilization of multiple conformations of AtAtm3 with MgADP-VO4 contrasts with previous observations on NaAtm1, where only the closed conformation was observed.
source: The stabilization of multiple conformations of AtAtm3 with MgADP-VO4 contrasts with our previous observations on NaAtm1, where only the closed conformation was observed (Fan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous work supported by citation to Fan et al., 2020.

claim: Structural differences between detergents and nanodiscs have been previously reported for MsbA under MgADP-VO4 stabilizing conditions.
source: Structural differences between detergents and nanodiscs have been previously reported for MsbA under MgADP-VO4 stabilizing conditions (Mi et al., 2017; Ward et al., 2007), and in the functional analysis of other membrane proteins (Hänelt et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mi et al., 2017, Ward et al., 2007, and Hänelt et al., 2013.

claim: The primary differences between the two structures of inward-facing conformations of AtAtm3 are in the relative positioning of the NBDs.
source: The primary differences between the two structures of inward-facing conformations of AtAtm3 are in the relative positioning of the NBDs which are more widely separated in the apo structure relative to the GSSG-bound structure.
evidence: This is a structural comparison of the two inward-facing conformations.

claim: Similar substrate-induced NBD movements have been previously observed in MRP1 and ABCB1.
source: Similar substrate-induced NBD movements have been previously observed in MRP1 (Johnson and Chen, 2017) and ABCB1 (Barbieri et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Johnson and Chen, 2017 and Barbieri et al., 2021.

claim: Kinked TM6s were observed in the inward-facing and closed state of AtAtm3, but not the outward-facing conformation.
source: As noted for NaAtm1, we observed kinked TM6s in the inward-facing and closed state of AtAtm3 (Figure 2cdh), but not the outward-facing conformation (Figure 2i).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2c,d,h,i.

claim: The cavity volume of the inward-facing apo structure was measured to be ~6500 Å3.
source: Using the program CastP (Tian et al., 2018) with a probe radius of 2.5 Å, the cavity volumes of the inward-facing apo and GSSG-bound structures were measured to be ~6500 Å3 (Figure 3a) and ~4300 Å3 (Figure 3b), respectively, while the closed conformation exhibits a cavity volume of ~300 Å3 (Figure 3c), and the outward-facing conformation has a cavity volume of ~5700 Å3 (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement using CastP shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The cavity volume of the GSSG-bound inward-facing structure was measured to be ~4300 Å3.
source: Using the program CastP (Tian et al., 2018) with a probe radius of 2.5 Å, the cavity volumes of the inward-facing apo and GSSG-bound structures were measured to be ~6500 Å3 (Figure 3a) and ~4300 Å3 (Figure 3b), respectively, while the closed conformation exhibits a cavity volume of ~300 Å3 (Figure 3c), and the outward-facing conformation has a cavity volume of ~5700 Å3 (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement using CastP shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The closed conformation exhibits a cavity volume of ~300 Å3.
source: Using the program CastP (Tian et al., 2018) with a probe radius of 2.5 Å, the cavity volumes of the inward-facing apo and GSSG-bound structures were measured to be ~6500 Å3 (Figure 3a) and ~4300 Å3 (Figure 3b), respectively, while the closed conformation exhibits a cavity volume of ~300 Å3 (Figure 3c), and the outward-facing conformation has a cavity volume of ~5700 Å3 (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement using CastP shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The outward-facing conformation has a cavity volume of ~5700 Å3.
source: Using the program CastP (Tian et al., 2018) with a probe radius of 2.5 Å, the cavity volumes of the inward-facing apo and GSSG-bound structures were measured to be ~6500 Å3 (Figure 3a) and ~4300 Å3 (Figure 3b), respectively, while the closed conformation exhibits a cavity volume of ~300 Å3 (Figure 3c), and the outward-facing conformation has a cavity volume of ~5700 Å3 (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement using CastP shown in Figure 3d.

claim: The cavity volume measurements for AtAtm3 are comparable to those calculated for NaAtm1.
source: Further, the cavity volume measurements are comparable to those calculated for NaAtm1 (Fan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous work supported by citation to Fan et al., 2020.

claim: The binding pocket for GSSG primarily consists of residues from TM5 and TM6, with additional contributions from residues in TM3 and TM4.
source: The binding pocket for GSSG identified in this work primarily consists of residues from TM5 and TM6, with additional contributions from residues in TM3 and TM4 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The GSSG binding site for AtAtm3 largely overlaps with that identified previously for NaAtm1 and for the binding of reduced GSH to ScAtm1.
source: The GSSG binding site for AtAtm3 largely overlaps with that identified previously for NaAtm1 (Lee et al., 2014) and for the binding of reduced GSH to ScAtm1 (Srinivasan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous work supported by citations to Lee et al., 2014 and Srinivasan et al., 2014.

claim: Residues forming the glutathione binding site are largely conserved among Atm1 homologs, particularly if they are involved in polar interactions.
source: Inspection of a sequence alignment of Atm1 homologs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) reveals that those residues forming the glutathione binding site are largely conserved, particularly if they are involved in polar interactions.
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is a stretch of residues from P432 to R441 in the middle of TM6 with sequence PLNFLGSVYR with a high degree of sequence conservation.
source: A striking feature is the stretch of residues from P432 to R441 in the middle of TM6 (AtAtm3 sequence numbering) with sequence PLNFLGSVYR with a high degree of sequence conservation.
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data.

claim: P432 is associated with the TM6 kink in inward-facing conformations that permits formation of hydrogen bonds between exposed peptide groups with GSSG.
source: P432 is associated with the TM6 kink in inward-facing conformations that permits formation of hydrogen bonds between exposed peptide groups with GSSG (Lee et al., 2014); as TM6 straightens in the occluded and outward-facing conformations, these peptide groups are no longer available to bind the transport substrate (Fan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2014 and Fan et al., 2020.

claim: Residues in the binding pockets are conserved among AtAtm3, NaAtm1, ScAtm1, and human ABCB7 and ABCB6 transporters, including T317, R324, R328, N387, Q390, L433, G437, and R441.
source: A sequence alignment of the structurally characterized AtAtm3, NaAtm1, ScAtm1, and human ABCB7 and ABCB6 transporters establishes that residues in the binding pockets are conserved, including T317, R324, R328, N387, Q390, L433, G437, and R441 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The conservation of binding pocket residues suggests that the substrates for these transporters may share common features, such as the glutathione backbone.
source: The conservation of binding pocket residues as calculated by the program ConSurf (Landau et al., 2005) is illustrated in Figure 4 suggests that the substrates for these transporters may share common features, such as the glutathione backbone.
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence conservation shown in Figure 4.

claim: Disulfide containing compounds such as GSSG can undergo disulfide-thiol exchange with free -SH groups.
source: An important property of disulfide containing compounds such as GSSG is that they can undergo disulfide – thiol exchange with free -SH groups (Creighton, 1984; Nagy, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Creighton, 1984 and Nagy, 2013.

claim: Reaction of a disulfide containing ligand such as GSSG with the thiol-containing side chain of cysteine could lead to formation of a mixed disulfide, thereby covalently connecting glutathione to the protein and releasing reduced GSH.
source: This reactivity creates potential challenges for proteins such as AtAtm3 since reaction of a disulfide containing ligand such as GSSG with the thiol-containing side chain of cysteine could lead to formation of the mixed disulfide, thereby covalently connecting glutathione to the protein and releasing reduced GSH.
evidence: This is an inference based on the chemical reactivity of disulfides.

claim: Formation of the covalently linked mixed disulfide would be expected to restrict the access of exogenous ligands to the substrate binding cavity and hence would inhibit transport.
source: Formation of the covalently linked mixed disulfide would be expected to restrict the access of exogenous ligands to the substrate binding cavity and hence would inhibit transport.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional consequences of mixed disulfide formation.

claim: Cysteine residues are present in TMs with a frequency of about 1%.
source: For membrane proteins, cysteine residues are present in TMs with a frequency of about 1% (Baeza-Delgado et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Baeza-Delgado et al., 2013.

claim: No cysteine residues are present in the AtAtm3 binding pocket.
source: Although no cysteines residues are present in the AtAtm3 binding pocket, we analyzed additional Atm3 homologs from plants.
evidence: This is a finding from structural analysis of AtAtm3.

claim: Within the six TMs of plant Atm3 homologs, the overall presence of cysteines was found to be ~0.4%.
source: Within the six TMs, the overall presence of cysteines was found to be ~0.4%.
evidence: This is a finding from sequence analysis of 410 Atm3 homologs.

claim: No cysteines were found in residues forming the glutathione binding cavity in the alignment of plant Atm3 homologs.
source: In this alignment, no cysteines were found in residues forming the glutathione binding cavity (Figure 5); more strikingly, no cysteine residues were found at any position of TM6 for these homologs (Figure 5f).
evidence: This is a finding from sequence analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: No cysteine residues were found at any position of TM6 for plant Atm3 homologs.
source: In this alignment, no cysteines were found in residues forming the glutathione binding cavity (Figure 5); more strikingly, no cysteine residues were found at any position of TM6 for these homologs (Figure 5f).
evidence: This is a finding from sequence analysis shown in Figure 5f.

claim: The observed exclusion of cysteines from the glutathione binding site could be the result of a selection against this residue to prevent the formation of inhibitory mixed disulfides during the transport cycle.
source: The observed exclusion of cysteines from the glutathione binding site (Figure 5g) could consequently be the result of a selection against this residue to prevent the formation of inhibitory mixed disulfides during the transport cycle.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sequence analysis shown in Figure 5g.

claim: MgADP-VO4 stabilized both a closed conformation in MSP nanodiscs and an outward-facing conformation in detergent for AtAtm3.
source: As a general strategy to stabilize ABC transporters in distinct conformational states, different nucleotides or transport substrates are mixed with the transporter. The expectation is that a particular set of ligands will stabilize a specific conformational state, and so we were surprised to have captured with MgADP-VO4 both a closed conformation in MSP nanodiscs and an outward-facing conformation in detergent.
evidence: This is a finding from structural studies of AtAtm3.

claim: The distinctive arrangements of the TMDs between the closed and outward-facing conformations presumably arise from differences in the TMD environment provided by MSP nanodiscs and DDM.
source: Given the similarities in the NBDs between these two structures, the distinctive arrangements of the TMDs between the closed and outward-facing conformations presumably arise from differences in the TMD environment provided by MSP nanodiscs and DDM, respectively.
evidence: This is an inference about the cause of conformational differences.

claim: Previously determined structures of MgADP-VO4 stabilized ABC exporters include NaAtm1 in the closed conformation, TmrAB in the occluded and outward-facing conformations, and MsbA in the closed conformation.
source: Furthermore, this phenomenon of obtaining different conformational states with MgADP-VO4 is not unprecedented, however, since previously determined structures of MgADP-VO4 stabilized ABC exporters include NaAtm1 in the closed conformation (Fan et al., 2020), Thermus thermophilus TmrAB in the occluded and outward-facing conformations (Hofmann et al., 2019), and E. coli MsbA in the closed conformation (Mi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fan et al., 2020, Hofmann et al., 2019, and Mi et al., 2017.

claim: The conformations of 80 half-transporters from the available structures of type IV ABC transporters were systematically compared.
source: Despite extensive efforts, we were unable to prepare the ternary complex of AtAmt3 with both bound GSSG and MgATP. To assess more generally the relationship between the conformational states of ABC exporters and the presence or absence of nucleotide and transport substrate, we systematically compared the conformations of 80 half-transporters from the available structures of type IV ABC transporters (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a description of the PCA analysis performed in the study.

claim: The structures were mapped onto a one-dimensional conformational axis using principal component analysis (PCA).
source: To guide this analysis, the structures were mapped onto a one-dimensional conformational axis using principal component analysis (PCA; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of the method used for analysis.

claim: The principal component is dominated by the conformational state of the TMDs, which represents ~62% of total conformational change from the inward-facing to the outward-facing conformation.
source: The principal component is dominated by the conformational state of the TMDs, which represents ~62% of total conformational change from the inward-facing to the outward-facing conformation.
evidence: This is a finding from the PCA analysis.

claim: Outward-facing conformations occur on the right-handed side of the PCA plot with component 1 values between –25 and 0 Å2.
source: It is evident that outward-facing conformations occur on the right-handed side of the figure with component 1 values between –25 and 0 Å2, while occluded, closed, and inward-facing conformations cluster around −25,–25, and –100 Å2, respectively.
evidence: This is a finding from the PCA analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Occluded, closed, and inward-facing conformations cluster around −25, –25, and –100 Å2, respectively, in the PCA plot.
source: It is evident that outward-facing conformations occur on the right-handed side of the figure with component 1 values between –25 and 0 Å2, while occluded, closed, and inward-facing conformations cluster around −25,–25, and –100 Å2, respectively.
evidence: This is a finding from the PCA analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Occluded and outward-facing conformations are largely nucleotide bound with either ATP or an ATP analog.
source: This analysis establishes that occluded and outward-facing conformations are largely nucleotide bound with either ATP or an ATP analog, but there are exceptions, most notably the original ADP-bound structure of Sav1866 in the outward facing conformation (Dawson and Locher, 2006; a similar Sav1866 structure was subsequently solved with bound AMPPNP; Dawson and Locher, 2007).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the PCA analysis shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Inward-facing conformations are observed in both nucleotide-free and nucleotide-bound forms.
source: Inward-facing conformations are observed in both nucleotide-free and nucleotide-bound forms (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the PCA analysis shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Only the MgADP-VO4-bound structures are exclusively found to occupy a small conformational space in the closed/outward-facing region.
source: Only the MgADP-VO4-bound structures are exclusively found to occupy a small conformational space in the closed/outward-facing region.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the PCA analysis shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Transport substrates and related inhibitors invariably bind to transporters in the inward-facing conformation.
source: In contrast to the binding of nucleotides to all conformational states of these transporters, a distinct pattern is observed for the binding of transport substrates where the transporter invariably adopts the inward-facing conformation (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the PCA analysis shown in Figure 6c.

claim: No structures with associated (dimerized) NBDs to date have been published that contain both nucleotide and transport substrate.
source: Intriguingly, no structures with associated (dimerized) NBDs to date have been published that contain both nucleotide and transport substrate, suggesting that this ternary complex exists only transiently during the transport cycle.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the survey of type IV ABC transporter structures.

claim: Characterization of the ternary complex represents an outstanding gap in the mechanistic characterization of ABC exporters.
source: As this is a key intermediate for understanding how the binding of transport substrate stimulates the ATPase activity, characterization of the ternary complex represents an outstanding gap in the mechanistic characterization of ABC exporters.
evidence: This is an inference about the importance of the ternary complex.
